extracted.intended_audience: NASA Headquarters and Center staff who draft, review, or manage internal and external correspondence and communications (scientists, engineers, program/project managers, public/legislative affairs, records management, and correspondence liaisons)
extracted.subtask_description: Agency-level procedural requirements and style standards for preparing, routing, reviewing, and managing NASA internal and external correspondence and communications in paper and electronic formats. Covers management roles, timelines and routing, and detailed plain-language writing and formatting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCIC central management of Principal-addressed communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The OCIC, Headquarters Correspondence Management Office manages and controls incoming and outgoing, internal and external correspondence, communications, and mail addressed to or signed by the Principals of the Office of the Administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCIC serves as the Agency focal point for communications addressed to or signed by the Principals; manages, controls, and tracks communications requiring responses; establishes Agencywide guidelines, style and format, and provides editorial guidance; ensures quality editing and proofreading reflecting 'plain language.'

rubrics_metrics.name: OCIC responsibility for tracking and recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: OCIC manages a tracking system of accountability for incoming and outgoing correspondence and a recordkeeping system to ensure records are maintained per Federal guidelines and Agency Retention Schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes processing actions initiated by Principals, coordinating senior-level communications, and ensuring records meet prescribed Federal guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of QCL and CCL liaisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Associate Administrator must designate a Quality Control Liaison (QCL) and a Correspondence Control Liaison (CCL) to facilitate communications flow between Action Offices and OCIC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate Administrators must provide names to OCIC, update designations timely, and provide a POC for absences. Designations are required to ensure efficient processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: QCL responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The QCL reviews and edits Action Office responses for actions assigned by the OCIC and ensures responses for signature reflect Agency standards, format, and content; ensures signature packages are properly assembled and initials the Action Document Summary (ADS) to signify review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCIC will return all packages the QCL fails to initial; recommended to hand-carry or fax signature packages when submitting to OCIC.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCL responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCL serves as the focal point for correspondence and actions assigned to the Action Office by the OCIC and manages a tracking system of accountability for those actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CCL coordinates internal tracking and receipt of assigned actions from OCIC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action Office mailboxes and daily checking
rubrics_metrics.description: OCIC establishes mailboxes for each Action Office and uses them to dispatch correspondence management matters; each Action Office must check its mailbox at least once per business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mailboxes are the official channel for dispatch and receipt of OCIC correspondence management items.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-profile responses identification and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Action Offices must meet due dates for high-profile responses; OCIC notes special handling requirements and pertinent information in the 'Abstract' section of the Action Cover Mask to call attention to special handling, short due dates, or staff hours expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-profile examples include communications involving the White House, foreign dignitaries, or other senior officials; follow the Abstract instructions on the Action Cover Mask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due date establishment and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: OCIC establishes due dates; default is a 10-business-day timeframe when no due date is stated. If incoming correspondence specifies a date, OCIC uses that date. White House referrals have prescribed 15–25 business day windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action Offices must meet due dates; use referral-specific timelines when provided (e.g., White House).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions of due dates
rubrics_metrics.description: All due dates must be met; requests for extensions should be rare and must be specifically justified by the Action Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action Office must immediately notify its assigned OCIC Correspondence Analyst of potential delinquency; OCIC will coordinate and provide guidance and may coordinate extension requests with external organizations or with the Office of the Administrator as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature package submission and processing
rubrics_metrics.description: All packages for signature by the Principals of the Office of the Administrator must first go through the OCIC; incomplete or incorrect packages are returned. Do not carry packages directly to the Office of the Administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes processing of NASA Directives; OCIC reviews, processes, and returns incomplete packages; Action Offices should obtain required concurrences before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required concurrences on Action Document Summary (ADS)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Action Office must obtain all required concurrences on the ADS before submitting signature packages to OCIC and must review 'Info Offices' listed on the Action Cover Mask to determine appropriate concurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrences are required from cognizant Headquarters organizations when responses include data from other offices or Centers; OCIC recommends simultaneous hand-carry or faxing of package to expedite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution lists for correspondence to officials and directors
rubrics_metrics.description: Action Offices must include the most current distribution list in signature packages; OCIC will return packages if the distribution list is absent or incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the Correspondence Management Web site for the most current listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized writing (newspaper format and front-loading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with the most important information and decrease to the least important (follow the newspaper format). Think of one key sentence that expresses the main idea; put requests before justifications and conclusions before discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the key sentence when appropriate; for complex replies, begin with a general statement of purpose; be direct and avoid routine delays in getting to the point. When persuading, end strongly; when in doubt, offer assistance and a contact name/phone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoken style
rubrics_metrics.description: Write so that the writing sounds like people talking to people. Imagine your reader sitting across the desk; write to one typical reader using personal pronouns and everyday words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read drafts aloud to check tone; do not use contractions in formal writing; use the imperative mood for administrative procedures and instructions to achieve directness and avoid passive voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact writing (conciseness and eliminating delayers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give ideas no more words than they deserve; shorten paragraphs, sentences, clauses, and words; avoid constructions like 'it is' and 'there is' that delay meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorten wordy expressions (e.g., 'in order to' -> 'to'); beware of overuse of '-ly' adverbs; cut doublings and redundancies; prefer everyday words to pompous ones; use short, spoken transitions instead of bookish ones; avoid legalistic language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone (neutrality and courtesy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a neutral, nonpersonal tone in routine letters; subordinates may suggest but only superiors may direct; courtesy is required though warmth is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially careful with sensitive matters to preserve goodwill; avoid tactless phrasing and rubber-stamp endings that can offend or promise more than can be delivered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write positively
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid negative language; when possible express ideas positively because positive statements are usually clearer and briefer. Use negative statements only when cautioning the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform negative phrasings into positive ones (many examples provided); 'Yes' answers need little explanation, 'No' answers generally need explanation to avoid sounding brushoff; use positive phrasing to soften bad news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, disciplined sentences and parallel structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Readable sentences are simple, active, affirmative, and declarative. State one thing per sentence; average 20 words or less; use parallel structure for lists and sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide long sentences; any sentence over 30 words should be perfectly parallel; remove unnecessary words; place key ideas at the sentence ends or beginnings for emphasis; use questions for emphasis where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short paragraphs and topic unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short, compact paragraphs—each paragraph should deal with a single, unified topic; long paragraphs impede reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short paragraphs especially at the beginning of letters; present complex material in related paragraphs or appendices; display lists and instructions with subparagraphs or bullets but avoid too many nesting levels; occasionally use one-sentence paragraphs to highlight important ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal pronouns appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal pronouns help clarify 'who' and retain reader interest. Use 'we/us/our' for the Agency or office, 'I/me/my' sparingly for the writer, and 'you' for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid referring to the Agency as 'it'; use 'I' less often and only for special concern or warmth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Active voice eliminates confusion by naming the actor and clarifying responsibility. Use a who-does-what order; avoid passive voice which makes sentences longer and actors unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use passive only when the actor is unknown, unimportant, or obvious; examples show how passive obscures responsibility and how active phrasing forces clarity (e.g., 'The messenger will deliver the material' vs. passive alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use action verbs and avoid nominals
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer action verbs to nominalized expressions (nouns formed from verbs) because verbs are shorter and more direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace cumbersome phrases (e.g., 'give consideration to' -> 'consider', 'make payment' -> 'pay'); avoid '-ion of', '-ment of', and '-ize of' forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain words; avoid jargon and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Government writing should be dignified but rely on plain language. Avoid jargon, pretentious expressions, and unnecessary words; prefer concrete words and avoid antagonizing terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many 'do not say / say' examples are provided (e.g., 'utilize' -> 'use', 'in order to' -> 'to'); avoid redundancies and noun sandwiches; use gender-neutral terminology; know precise meanings and use of 'must/shall/will/should/may/may not'; avoid split infinitives where possible; use 'that' vs 'which' correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acronym usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use acronyms more than necessary. Spell out an acronym the first time it appears followed by the acronym in parentheses; capitalize the first letter of each word in the acronym as cited in Appendix H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an acronym appears only twice or infrequently, spell out the term every time or avoid the acronym entirely. Example: Flight Readiness Review (FRR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer/Internet word usage and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescribe preferred capitalization and forms for Internet/computer terms: Internet, Net (initial cap); World Wide Web / WWW / Web / the Web (initial cap W); Web site and Web page (two words, initial cap W); Home Page (two words, initial cap when referring to a site).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study The Gregg Reference Manual appendix on computer terms when preparing communications with such words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classified correspondence: safeguards, format, transmission, addressing
rubrics_metrics.description: Classified correspondence requires safeguards and controls, specific equipment and supplies, particular formats and marking, rules for transmission, and specific addressing conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CHAPTER 8 headings indicate requirements for safeguards and controls, format/marking, transmission, and addressing; follow applicable security and classification policies (e.g., Executive Order No. 12958 and agency security policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formats and assemblies for letters and memorandums
rubrics_metrics.description: There are prescribed formats for Standard Business Letters, Nonpersonalized Business Letters, Legal Letters, Multiple-Addressee Letters, Standard Memos, Memorandum for the Record, and procedures for assembling documents for signature, envelopes, and mailing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the chapter-format templates and assembly instructions (including enclosures and distribution) to ensure consistency and proper routing for signature and mailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic communications rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic communications (e-mail, facsimile, telex, NASCOM messages, and other services) have general rules and style/guidance distinct from paper correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Chapter 6 guidance for electronic mail communications, fax usage, telex, NASCOM formats, and other communications services; ensure security and records considerations are observed.
